newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Zaire rebel leader meets S.Africa's Mandela.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebel leader meets S.Africa's Mandela.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila met President Nelson Mandela on Thursday as South Africa redoubled its efforts to avert a bloody civil war showdown in Zaire's capital Kinshasa.

Kabila arrived in Cape Town on a South African jet several hours behind schedule at sunset and was driven straight to Mandela's Tuynhuys office, where he was ushered directly into a one-on-one meeting.
Presidential spokesman Parks Mankahlana said Mandela and Kabila would be joined later by United Nations envoy Mohamed Sahnoun to discuss the details of a South African peace plan.
"We have reason to be optimistic," he said.
Mandela failed on Wednesday to broker a face-to-face meeting between Kabila and Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko aboard a South African navy icebreaker in the Congolese port of Pointe Noire.
Kabila, citing security fears, kept Mandela and Mobutu waiting for several hours and then refused to fly to the ship.
South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, a key negotiator in the Zairean peace initiative, had said Wednesday's meeting could be Zaire's last chance for peace.
But on Thursday he and Mandela renewed their initiative, urging African and Western leaders to help rescue the talks and sending the jet to pick up Kabila in the Angolan enclave of Cabinda.
"The humanitarian tragedy unfolding in Zaire is unprecedented. There is no amount of patience he (Mandela) cannot find. He is compelled to continue," said Mankahlana.
"We think there is still a very large opening for them both to walk through to achieve peace in Zaire," he said.

Mobutu, fighting cancer and the encircling grip of Kabila's rebel alliance, returned to Kinshasa on Thursday. Witnesses said he spurned a red carpet farewell and honour guard laid on by the Congolese and boarded his plane by a rear entrance.
Zaire's teeming capital grew more tense by the hour on Thursday as people braced for what many now believe is the inevitable battle for Kinshasa.
With peace talks stalled, the city of five million was left facing the prospects of a military assault by rebel troops and an orgy of looting by retreating soldiers.
Shops were shuttered and the normally bustling streets emptied ominously well before sundown and a third night of military curfew. The airport was effectively closed.
"We're heading directly for a bloodbath. It's a question of balance of forces. Kabila knows he has the upper hand," said Mobutu aide Kabuya Lumuna.
In a message broadcast by BBC World Service radio, the British Foreign Office urged British and Commonwealth nationals to leave the capital while commercial transport was available.
"The situation is increasingly volatile in the Kinshasa area," the broadcast said.
On the roof of the French embassy in downtown Kinshasa diplomatic staff were seen burning what appeared to be shredded documents.
A member of the Organisation of African Unity delegation in Pointe Noire told reporters on Thursday the OAU was very pessimistic about prospects for a negotiated peace.
Mbeki told reporters South Africa would discuss with Kabila a rebel warning to Mobutu to quit the capital before Saturday or risk capture by advancing forces.

Lisbon's Lusa news agency had earlier quoted rebel justice spokesman Mwenze Kongolo as saying: "The only way out of the crisis is for Mobutu to hand over power to the armed rebellion which will form a transitional government together with other forces fighting for the same cause."
Mankahlana said Mandela was trying to get Mobutu, who has ruled Zaire for 32 years, and Kabila to ratify his plan to end Zaire's civil war and ensure a peaceful transition to democracy.
The South African Broadcasting Corporation, quoting a leaked copy of Mandela's proposal, said it would require Mobutu to step down within 24 hours of signing a settlement.
The European Parliament on Thursday urged Mobutu and Kabila to form an interim government to organise democratic elections.
